# AUDIO PROFILE: the house narrator is warm, grounded and quietly witty. Neutral American accent, light and natural, not announcer-y.
### DIRECTOR'S NOTES
Style: warm, grounded, curious and quietly witty. Make the remote measurement feel genuinely impressive. Let the map check land with confidence. Give the empty borehole a clean breath of silence. Finish as an invitation to the next field test, never as a warning.
Pace: MEASURED and unhurried. THIS IS A TWO MINUTE PIECE, about one hundred twenty seconds, and the read must FILL it, so give every sentence room to land and take a real breath at every period. Do not rush the numbers. Vary the tone line to line so no two sentences sound the same.
Emphasis: lean on one load-bearing word per line. Let twice, checked, split, real, modeled, no and underground land.
Transcript:
A mountain of rock near McCarthy sped up twice.
Not once in the study, but twice each year.
Sentinel One radar mapped seven rock glaciers near McCarthy from twenty eighteen through twenty twenty two.
They are rivers of rock and ice.
Parts of Sourdough Peak moved more than one hundred sixty centimeters a year.
A nearby glacier moved less than half as fast in the university summary.
Photogrammetry checked more than sixteen thousand Sourdough Peak pixels.
The maps correlated at point eight four two, with mean error of ten point seven two centimeters a year.
Researchers fixed two components. Unsupervised separation yielded a long crawl and seasonal pulse they interpreted.
That pulse peaked after snowmelt and again with later rain.
Four measured years lagged snowmelt by seventy two to eighty four days. Twenty nineteen used an estimated eighty four to ninety six day temperature proxy instead.
The measured surface signal is real. Is the explanation?
The authors modeled a path from sunlight to meltwater to a buried sliding layer.
No borehole temperatures were recorded. The weather station sat six kilometers away.
Two smaller glaciers broke the simple sunlight pattern.
That does not erase the measurement.
It turns the result into a sharper field test.
Put sensors underground. Watch the next melt and rain. See whether the mountain keeps both appointments.
